Certainly out of that whole will be also this which does not come into deformation. And above you declared that the whole of it was not fabricated. Therefore even this rough and confused and unformed thing cannot be recognized in things polished and distinct and composed — which it is not fitting even to call parts of Matter, since by alteration they have departed, divided from its form.

I return to motion, that everywhere I may show you slippery. Unfounded and unconfused and turbulent was the motion of Matter. For thus you set before us the likeness of a pot bubbling on every side. And how is another motion elsewhere affirmed by you? For when you wish to introduce Matter as neither good nor evil, Therefore, you say, the underlying Matter, having a motion of equal momentum, inclines greatly neither to good nor to evil. If of equal momentum, then it is no longer turbulent, nor pot-like, but composed and tempered — namely, that which, agitated of its own choice between good and evil, yet inclined and headlong to neither part, was borne with an even-balanced impulse, as they say, of a middle yoke. This you will say is not unevenness; this is not turbulence and passibility, but moderation and modesty and justice of a motion inclining to neither part. Plainly, if it inclined this way and that, or more to one side, then it would deserve to be marked for inconcinnity and inequality and turbulence. Further, if the motion was inclined neither to good nor to evil, surely it was carried on between good and evil — so that from this too Matter appears determinable, whose motion, inclined to neither evil nor good, in that it inclined to neither, hung within both and from both, and on this score was determined by both. But you also place good and evil in place, when you say the motion of Matter was inclined to neither of them. For Matter, which was in place, inclining neither this way nor that, did not incline into the places in which good and evil were. But by giving place to good and evil, you make them corporeal, by making them local; for things which have place must first be corporeal. In short, incorporeal things would not have a proper place except in a body, when they accede to a body. But Matter, not inclining to good and evil, did not incline to them as corporeal or local. You err, then, if you will have good and evil to be substances. For you make them substances to which you assign places; and you assign places when you suspend the motion of Matter from both regions.

You have scattered all things, lest, set side by side, they should shine out as contrary to each other. But I will gather the individual points and confer them. You assert the motion of Matter to be unfounded, and you add that it followed formlessness; then elsewhere, that it desired to be composed by God. Does that which follows formlessness desire formation? Or does that which desires formation follow formlessness? You will not have God seem equated to Matter, and yet you make it have communion with God. For it is impossible, you say, that it, not having something in common with God, should be adorned by him. But if it had something in common with God, it would not desire to be adorned by him, being, namely, a part of God through communion. Or God too could be adorned by Matter, having himself too something in common with it; and now in this you subject God to necessity, if there was something in Matter on account of which he should form it. But you make this common between them, that they are moved by themselves and are always moved. What less do you ascribe to Matter than to God? The whole consortium of divinity will be this: liberty and eternity of motion. But God is moved orderly, Matter unfoundedly. Yet it is likewise divine, by a motion likewise free and eternal. Nay, you give the more to Matter, to which it was permitted to be moved in a way in which it was not permitted to God.

Concerning motion I would have noted this too. For according to the likeness of the pot, you say, such was the motion of Matter before it was disposed — concrete, restless, ungraspable through the excess of its conflict. Then you subjoin, But it stood still for the composition of God, and the unfounded motion was ungraspable through the slowness of the unfounded motion. Above you ascribe conflict to the motion, here slowness. For take note how often you fall concerning the nature of Matter. Above you say, But if Matter were of an evil nature, it would not have admitted translation into the better, nor would God have accommodated anything of composition to it; for he would have laboured in vain. You have therefore concluded two sentences — that Matter is not of an evil nature, and that its nature could not be converted by God — forgetful of which you afterwards bring in: But when it received composition from God and was adorned, it ceased from its nature. If it was reformed into good, surely it was reformed from evil; and if through the composition of God it ceased from the nature of evil, then it ceased from its nature, and its nature was evil before composition, and it could cease from its nature after reformation.

But it follows that I should show in what manner you make God to have worked. Plainly you depart from the philosophers; but yet from the prophets too. For the Stoics will have it that God ran through Matter as honey through honeycombs. But you say, Not by passing through it does he make the world, but only by appearing and approaching it, as a beautiful thing acts by only appearing, and the magnet stone by only approaching. What likeness is there between God fabricating the world and beauty wounding the mind, or a magnet attracting iron? For even if God appeared to Matter, yet he did not wound it, as beauty the mind; and if he approached, yet he did not cleave to it, as the magnet to iron. Suppose now your examples were fitting. Certainly, if by appearing and approaching Matter God made the world out of it, then he made it from the time he appeared, and from the time he approached. Therefore, when he had not yet made it, he had neither appeared to it nor approached it. And to whom is it credible that God did not appear to Matter — even as consubstantial to his own through eternity? — that he was far from it whom we believe to be everywhere and everywhere to appear, to whom even inanimate and incorporeal things sing praises in Daniel? How great is this place in which God was so far distant from Matter that he neither appeared nor approached before the constructing of the world? I believe he made a pilgrimage to it from afar, when first he wished to appear and approach it.

But the prophets and apostles do not so hand down that the world was made by God, by his only appearing and approaching Matter; because they named no Matter at all, but first Wisdom founded, the beginning of the ways unto his works; then the Word brought forth, through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made. In short, by his word the heavens were established, and by his Spirit all their powers. This is the right hand of God and both his hands, through which he worked and constructed. For the works of your hands, he says, are the heavens — by which he both measured heaven and the earth with his span. Do not so flatter God as to wish that he brought forth so many and so great substances by mere seeing and mere approach, and did not establish them by his own powers. For thus too Jeremiah commends him: God making the earth in his strength, preparing the world in his understanding, and by his own sense he stretched out the heavens. These are his powers, by which, straining, he founded all this. His glory is the greater if he laboured. In short, on the seventh day he rested from his works. Each in its own manner. Or, if by only appearing and approaching he made this world — did he, when he ceased to make, again cease to appear and approach? On the contrary, God began the more to appear and to be met everywhere from the time the world was made. You see therefore how all things subsist by the operation of God — by the strength of him who makes the earth, by the understanding of him who prepares the world, and by the sense of him who stretches out heaven — not of one only appearing, nor approaching, but bringing to bear so great efforts of his mind: Wisdom, strength, sense, Word, Spirit, power. Which were not necessary to him if, by only appearing and approaching, he had been perfect. But these are his invisible things, which, according to the apostle, from the foundation of the world are perceived through the things he made — not some Matter or other, but his own sensible attributes. For who has known the mind of the Lord, of which he exclaims, O the depth of the riches and of the wisdom, how unsearchable are his judgements and his ways past finding out! What do these things more savour of than that all things were made out of nothing? — which could neither be found nor searched out except by God alone; otherwise they would be searchable, if they were searched out and found out of Matter. Therefore, in so far as it is established that there was no Matter — from this too, that it does not even fit that there was such a Matter as is introduced — to that same degree it is proved that all things were made by God out of nothing. Except that Hermogenes, by describing the same state for Matter in which he himself is — unfounded, confused, turbulent, of a doubtful and headlong and seething motion — while he shows a document of his art, has painted himself.
